opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the framing I find most useful is to imagine that the company doesn't particularly care about safety one way or the other. It's not actively hostile to it, and it's not a true believer either. It's just a big organization with a lot of competing priorities: shipping products, hitting revenue targets, keeping up with competitors, keeping employees happy. Safety is one consideration among many.

The reason I like this framing is that it pushes you toward proposals that actually work in practice. If you assume the company is deeply committed to safety, you might propose something that's costly, slows things down, and requires a lot of goodwill. That might get a nod in a meeting, but when deadlines hit and the tradeoffs get real, it quietly gets dropped. If you assume the company is adversarial, you tend to go straight to external pressure and regulation, which has its place, but you miss many things you could get done internally.

The apathetic framing asks a different question: what would a reasonable organization adopt even if it only cared a little? That points you toward interventions that are cheap, that fit into existing workflows, that have some side benefit like better product reliability or reduced legal or reputational risk, and that are easy to say yes to. It also makes you think hard about the burden of proof. You have to show concretely why the thing matters and what it costs, rather than assuming everyone already shares your worldview.

It's also more robust. Companies change. Leadership turns over, competitive pressure goes up, the people who championed safety move on. If your safety practices only survive because a few key people care deeply, they're fragile. If they survive because they're cheap and sensible enough that even an indifferent organization would keep them, they're much more likely to stick.

And honestly, I think it's a fairly accurate model of most large organizations most of the time. Individual people inside these companies often care a lot, but the organization as a whole behaves like something with many priorities and limited attention. So designing your advocacy around that reality tends to work better than designing it around the best case or the worst case.

r001.rationale: The response describes competing priorities and limited attention, but does not say those constraints limit the company to pursuing only a few safety initiatives at a time.

r002.rationale: It recommends changes that are cheap, fit existing workflows, offer side benefits, and are easy to accept, communicating that proposals should avoid disrupting other priorities.

fable-5.1.text:
Rohin Shah: So the frame I find useful is: assume the company is neither evil nor benevolent, just mostly indifferent. It has a bunch of goals it cares about, like shipping products, keeping customers happy, staying ahead of competitors, and safety is a thing it will do if it's cheap and easy, or if someone is pushing for it, but it's not going to spontaneously go out of its way for it.

I like this because I think it's actually closer to the truth than either of the alternative stories. If you model the company as actively malicious, you end up predicting that it'll resist every safety measure, and that's just not what happens. Lots of safety stuff gets done, often because a few people inside asked for it and nobody had a strong reason to say no. But if you model it as basically trying to do the right thing, you'll be surprised when something that seems obviously important just doesn't happen, because it wasn't anyone's job and it cost a bit of engineering time.

And then the apathy model gives you very concrete guidance about how to advocate. The key question becomes: how do I make this the path of least resistance? If I'm proposing a change, I should make it as cheap as possible, I should have already done the work to show it won't hurt the product, I should find the person whose metrics it actually helps. You're not trying to convince anyone that safety matters in the abstract, you're trying to reduce the cost of saying yes to below the cost of saying no.

It also tells you where the hard cases are. When a safety measure genuinely conflicts with something the company does care about, like a big delay to a launch, apathy isn't going to carry you. There you actually need external pressure, or regulation, or a leader who personally cares. So the model doesn't say everything is fine, it just helps you tell apart the stuff you can get done with a well-argued doc from the stuff that needs a different lever.

r001.rationale: The response lists competing company goals and says safety measures may be skipped if they cost time, but does not explain that these constraints limit the company to pursuing only a few safety initiatives at a time.

r002.rationale: It recommends showing that a proposed change “won’t hurt the product” and making it as cheap as possible, so it does not interfere with the company’s other priorities.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful because it pushes you to ask: what would make this change easy for the company to adopt? If you assume they’re already deeply committed to safety, you might expect them to make big sacrifices on the basis of an argument that you find compelling. If you assume they’re actively opposed to safety, you might conclude there’s no point engaging with them at all.

Treating them as apathetic gives you a more practical starting point: suppose they’re willing to do something safer, provided it doesn’t cost too much or interfere too much with what they’re trying to do. Can you offer a concrete proposal that fits those constraints? Can you reduce the engineering work required, or make the safety benefit easier to assess?

That doesn’t mean apathy is an accurate description of everyone at an AI company. It’s a useful assumption for designing your advocacy. You want the proposal to succeed without requiring everyone involved to share your level of concern.

r001.rationale: The response mentions limits such as cost and interference, but does not explain that those constraints restrict companies to pursuing only a few safety initiatives at a time.

r002.rationale: It recommends proposing a safety change that fits the company’s constraints and specifically asks whether it can avoid interfering with what the company is trying to do.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful because it pushes you to ask, “What would make this change easy for them to adopt?” If you imagine the company as actively opposed to safety, you can end up treating every disagreement as a fight. If you imagine that safety is already their overriding priority, you can end up surprised when they don’t do what you recommend.

Treating them as apathetic gives you a practical starting point: they have lots of competing priorities, and your proposal needs to make sense in that context. Can you make the safety benefit clear? Can you reduce the cost? Can you give someone a concrete thing to do, rather than saying, “You should take this problem more seriously”?

And I don’t mean that everyone at these companies is actually apathetic. There are people who care a lot. But even those people have limited time and need to persuade other people internally. Giving them a specific, feasible proposal is much more helpful than giving them another argument that safety matters.

r001.rationale: The response mentions competing priorities and limited time, but does not explain that these constraints limit companies to pursuing only a few safety initiatives at a time.

r002.rationale: It recommends making proposals clear, feasible, and less costly, but does not clearly recommend showing that a change will not interfere with the company’s other priorities.
